B instead defines 'addressed' itself as generation-relative: 'a tile is *addressed* in a generation if that generation's tile index has an entry for it: the tiles of the layer's grid under the geometry that generation declares'. This matters because dimension extents can grow across generations (confirmed elsewhere in both editions, e.g. the append procedure's growth rules), so the set of tiles that exist in a layer's grid is not fixed for all generations of a layer - A's literal wording ('every tile of a layer is addressed', unqualified) is imprecise about which generation's grid is meant, while B's wording resolves that ambiguity explicitly. Neither edition attaches a requirement ID to this glossary bullet, and the operative rules that actually determine which tiles exist for a given generation (section 11.2 Grid arithmetic, section 15 Tile Index, and the growth clause of section 20.3's append procedure) are byte-identical between editions, so no concrete file's conformance verdict changes.
findings.quotation_a: **addressed tile / stored tile** — every tile of a layer is *addressed*. A tile is *stored in a generation* if and only if that generation's tile-index entry for it is not the sentinel (§15); unqualified *stored* means stored in the live generation.
findings.quotation_b: **addressed tile / stored tile** — a tile is *addressed* in a generation if that generation's tile index has an entry for it: the tiles of the layer's grid under the geometry that generation declares (§11.2, §15). It is *stored in a generation* if and only if that entry is not the sentinel (§15); unqualified *stored* means stored in the live generation.

The single divergence (quiza-quiza-q14) asks whether index_encoding = 0x50 (reserved 2-0x7F) and index_encoding = 0x90 (experimental >= 0x80) fall under the same register row/outcome or different ones. Both takers answered the same substantive thing: a single shared row, L31, with outcome reject-layer (validity error at layer scope). Taker A wrote the row id "L31" and quoted the register-row text without its leading "L31 |" cell marker; taker B wrote "Same row: L31" and quoted the same text with the marker included. These are the same answer in different words, not two different findings.

B's section 7.1 states only the directory-CRC rule; the entire framing paragraph is moved, with every clause intact including the '5 bytes' figure and the resource-decline exception, into B's section 7.3. findings.quotation_a: An extent of (0, 0) on a user-metadata record, or one whose extent_length is less than 5 — too short to hold both a document and the terminal CRC-32C §8.1 places in its final 4 bytes — is a validity error at its containing scope.
findings.quotation_b: On a user-metadata record, an extent slot of (0, 0) or an extent_length less than 5 is a validity error at its containing scope: fewer than 5 bytes cannot hold both a document and the terminal CRC-32C §8.1 places in the final 4.
findings.byte_level_rationale: The rule, figures and exceptions are unchanged; only its section location moved, so an implementation built from either edition enforces the identical extent-slot and extent_length constraints on a user-metadata record.

findings.title: Checksum-coverage exceptions list relocated from section 4.5 to section 8.1 in B, verified lossless
findings.detail: A states R-ENC-10 followed immediately by a full enumeration of the three coverage exceptions (front signature block checked by equality; terminal checksum fields verified by comparison; unassigned-record-type extents covered by no checksum) plus the interior-checksum-fields rule, all inside section 4.5. B's section 4.5 drops this enumeration entirely after R-ENC-10, but restates it in full, with the same three-exceptions structure and the same interior-fields clause, as new prose opening B's section 8.1 (which in A states only the coverage table with no restated prose enumeration). Every clause of A's section-4.5 enumeration is present, unchanged in substance, in B's section 8.1.
findings.quotation_a: Every field of every structure is covered by exactly one checksum, excepting the front signature block (a constant whose check is equality, §6), the terminal checksum fields of §8.1's map — the trailer, directory-region, and user-metadata checksum fields — which are verified by comparison and covered by no further checksum, and the extent of a record of a type this specification has not assigned, which §8.1's map covers by no checksum at all.
findings.quotation_b: Every field of every structure is covered by exactly one checksum, as this map states, with three exceptions. The front signature block is checked by byte equality (§6.1). This map's terminal checksum fields, which are the trailer's, the directory region's and the user-metadata extent's, are verified by comparison and covered by no further checksum. The extent of a record of a type this specification has not assigned is covered by no checksum at all...
findings.byte_level_rationale: The coverage-exception rule is identical in substance and relocated, not cut; §8.1's coverage table itself (listing exactly which bytes each checksum covers) is byte-identical in both editions, so no implementation detail changes.

findings.title: R1 walkers cite different requirement IDs (R-ENC-05/10 vs R-CNT-11) for the same identical open-accounting text
findings.detail: Walker A answers R1 by citing section 4.5's R-ENC-05 ('MUST NOT allocate, seek, or issue I/O... before the checksum covering it has been verified') and R-ENC-10 for why dir_offset/dir_length cannot bound request 2 before the trailer CRC verifies. Walker B cites section 7.1's R-CNT-11 (the directory CRC rule itself) for the same point. Both requirement IDs, and the underlying section 6.4/6.2 open-accounting text, are byte-for-byte identical between editions (confirmed directly), so this is a difference in which equally-valid rule each walker chose to cite, not a text difference between A and B.
findings.quotation_a: A reader MUST NOT allocate, seek, or issue I/O based on any integer obtained from a file before the checksum covering it has been verified (§4.5, §8). `[R-ENC-05]`
findings.quotation_b: A reader MUST NOT allocate, seek, or issue I/O based on any integer obtained from a file before the checksum covering it has been verified (§4.5, §8). `[R-ENC-05]`
findings.byte_level_rationale: Both editions contain R-ENC-05, R-ENC-10, and R-CNT-11 verbatim-identically; the two-request, 64+dir_length byte accounting that R1 asks about is identical in both, so no implementation built from either edition alone differs in the bytes it fetches or the order it fetches them in.

findings.location_a: R8: section 21.2 register rows F35, F36 (A:3879-3880)
findings.location_b: R8: section 21.2 register rows F35, F36 (B:3735-3736)
findings.title: R8 walkers cite different register rows (F35/F36 vs F36 alone) for the same identical rows in both editions
findings.detail: Walker A's R8 answer cites 'register F35/F36 if the type value is in the reserved range' for the top-level unimplemented-type case. Walker B's D1 degradation walk cites 'register row F36, detector verifier' specifically for the independent file-nonconformance ground (distinct from F35's reader-detected reject-file at open). Both F35 and F36 exist, byte-for-byte identically worded, at the same relative position in both editions' section 21.2. This is a difference in which row each walker emphasizes for which sub-point, not a textual divergence between editions.
findings.quotation_a: F35 | A top-level record has a reserved-range type value (0x0003-0x7FFF, §10.2) with MUST_UNDERSTAND (flags bit 0) set to 1 | — | reader | open | `[R-CNT-15]`
findings.quotation_b: F36 | A top-level record carries a type value from the reserved range 0x0003-0x7FFF, which this specification has not assigned; emitting one is a violation whatever its MU bit | — | verifier | certification | `[R-CNT-15]`
findings.byte_level_rationale: Both register rows are present, worded identically, in both editions, so an implementation built from either edition alone applies the same reject-file-at-open (F35) and same verifier-detected-nonconformance (F36) outcomes to the same byte patterns.

findings.title: All eight probes (R1-R8): cited passages equivalent or identical in both editions; walkers agree correctly, not by luck
findings.detail: For R3, R4, R6, and R7, the specific passages each walker cites are byte-for-byte identical between editions (confirmed by direct line-range comparison), so the two walks' agreement on these probes is not coincidental but follows necessarily from reading the same text. For R1, R2, R5, and R8, the passages are substantively equivalent (rewording, sentence-splitting, or content relocated to a different section but fully preserved), and the walkers' agreement again follows from the underlying rules being unchanged. No probe showed one edition stating a rule the other does not state somewhere, and no walker's answer depended on a passage that the other edition omits or narrows.
findings.quotation_a: see individual probe entries in the transcript (section 1)
findings.quotation_b: see individual probe entries in the transcript (section 1)
findings.byte_level_rationale: Since the cited text is identical or equivalent across all eight probes, no implementation built from one edition alone would diverge from one built from the other on any of the eight probed scenarios.

findings.location_a: §20.3 step 4 (forbidden fixed-declaration changes paragraph, R-WRT-04 context) + §21.7, cited in W6
findings.location_b: §20.3 step 4 (same passage, byte-identical) + §21.7 (same), cited in W6 and finding writerb-04
findings.title: Writer-b misreads the shared, edition-identical T4 exception as excluding fill changes
findings.detail: Both editions state, identically: '...with every checksum in §8 certifying the result and, but for a stored tile's decoded size, a padding position or pad bit, or a boolean byte the register witnesses (T3, T14, T21, T22, T4, T5, T2)... no check any actor owes able to see it (§21.7).' T4 is the padding-content rule (padding bytes must equal the declared fill), so a forbidden fill-only change on a layer that HAS padding positions is witnessed by T4; only a layer with zero padding positions escapes detection entirely. Writer-a (from A) derives exactly this conditional and marks it [underdetermined] on the padding fact. Writer-b (from B), reading the byte-identical sentence, quotes the same T-number list including T4 but then asserts unconditionally 'a fill change alone is not in that named list' and that the change is 'in fact unwitnessed' (repeated in finding writerb-04) — misreading the very passage it cites, which names T4 as exactly the check that sees this case when padding exists.
findings.quotation_a: "...with every checksum in §8 certifying the result and, but for a stored tile's decoded size, a padding position or pad bit, or a boolean byte the register witnesses (T3, T14, T21, T22, T4, T5, T2) and a decode that fails outright, or a codec's framing check that precedes it, under a changed codec or filter (T17, T24, T25), no check any actor owes able to see it (§21.7)."
findings.quotation_b: "...with every checksum in §8 certifying the result and, but for a stored tile's decoded size, a padding position or pad bit, or a boolean byte the register witnesses (T3, T14, T21, T22, T4, T5, T2) and a decode that fails outright, or a codec's framing check that precedes it, under a changed codec or filter (T17, T24, T25), no check any actor owes able to see it (§21.7)."
findings.byte_level_rationale: Edition is immaterial here since the text is identical, but the stakes are real: a verifier implemented from writer-b's stated rule would skip the T4 padding-content check for a layer whose fill was changed by a forbidden direct commit, and so would certify as conforming a file that a verifier correctly implementing T4 (as writer-a's answer implies) would reject at layer scope for a padding byte that no longer equals the newly declared fill.

findings.location_a: §2.3 Conforming-verifier bullet (inline grounds list + adjacent disclaimer)
findings.location_b: §2.3 Conforming-verifier bullet (shortened, forward-pointing) + new paragraph at end of §21.6
findings.title: B relocates the "cannot establish" grounds list and drops its adjacent experimental-range disclaimer, which survives only elsewhere
findings.detail: A states the five 'cannot establish' grounds inline in §2.3 and immediately appends: 'A user-metadata document under an experimental-range encoding...is not such a ground: no content rule attaches there, so nothing is left unchecked, and certification is unaffected (R-MTA-10); encoding 0 and a reserved value are violations (§21.5, R1).' B shortens §2.3 to 'cannot establish...(§21.6 names the grounds)' and instead adds a new paragraph at the end of §21.6 (confirmed absent from A) restating the same five grounds, including 'declines to decode a user-metadata document (R-MTA-09),' WITHOUT the adjacent disclaimer. The disclaimer is not actually lost: it survives, byte-identical, in §21.5's prose and in §21.6's own Conditions-table R1 row in both editions. So B's complete text still determines the same verdict as A, but a reader of only the new, locally-added paragraph lacks the one qualification most relevant to the ground it names last.
findings.quotation_a: "...or when it declines to decode a user-metadata document ([R-MTA-09]). A user-metadata document under an experimental-range encoding — one this specification does not assign and a conforming file can carry (§21.6) — is not such a ground: no content rule attaches there, so nothing is left unchecked, and certification is unaffected ([R-MTA-10]); encoding 0 and a reserved value are violations (§21.5, R1)."
findings.quotation_b: "A verifier is unable to check a requirement on a capability or resource ground, and so reports *cannot establish* ([R-CNF-11]), as when the file names a format major version it does not implement, a record carries MUST_UNDERSTAND = 1 with a type it does not implement, it cannot execute a codec or filter ([R-COD-11], §17.4), it declines a layer's or a tile's decode on resource grounds and so cannot check §14's decoded-content obligations ([R-ERR-04], [R-SER-05], [R-SER-08]), or it declines to decode a user-metadata document ([R-MTA-09])."
findings.byte_level_rationale: No divergence for an implementer who reads either edition's full text, since the disclaiming rule survives unchanged in both editions' §21.5 prose and §21.6 table row. The risk is confined to a reader who stops at the single newly-added paragraph in B without following its own citations into §21.5/§21.6.

findings.location_a: §2.3 Conforming-updater and Conforming-verifier bullets (both byte-identical to B)
findings.title: Writerb-01's updater/verifier ambiguity is shared by both editions verbatim; only writer-a's engagement with it differs
findings.detail: Writer-b's finding writerb-01 notes a tension between the updater bullet's 'without necessarily understanding all of its content' and the verifier bullet's 'Verifiers and updaters are readers of the files they process and inherit every reader obligation' (which textually includes R-CNF-03's no-subset-profiles mandate). Both sentences are byte-identical in A and B (confirmed by direct comparison), so this is not a fidelity difference between editions. Writer-a's own transcript explicitly considered and rejected this exact scenario for W8 without quoting or engaging the 'inherit every reader obligation' sentence that creates the tension; writer-b quotes and engages it directly. Both walkers reach the same ultimate W8 answer (carry the layer forward, checksum-only), so no probe answer is wrong — the difference is diligence in surfacing a textual tension that exists equally in both editions.
findings.quotation_a: "A tool that modifies an existing file, or as a rewriter writes a new one from it (§20.1), without necessarily understanding all of its content... Verifiers and updaters are readers of the files they process and inherit every reader obligation."
findings.quotation_b: "A tool that modifies an existing file, or as a rewriter writes a new one from it, without necessarily understanding all of its content... Verifiers and updaters are readers of the files they process and inherit every reader obligation."
findings.byte_level_rationale: No divergence between editions: the ambiguity, if it has any practical bite, is a defect shared identically by A and B, not something B's rewrite introduced or removed.

findings.title: A states a conforming file's unimplemented-type/MU=1 record is necessarily experimental-range; B never states this
findings.detail: Edition A's 'conforming reader' bullet contains the clause 'in a conforming file such a type is necessarily from the experimental range, since a reserved-range type carrying MU = 1 is itself a violation' (A line 183), directly resolving, at the point the obligation is defined, probe V2's reserved-vs-experimental fork for any file with no other established violation. Edition B's corresponding bullet omits this clause entirely, and the sentence does not exist anywhere else in B (grep -n "necessarily from the experimental" spec/tarn.md returns 0 hits; the identical pattern against edition A returns 1, confirming the search itself works). This is the direct textual cause of the V2 divergence: verifier-A quoted A's sentence and answered both branches without hedging; verifier-B, reading text that never states it, flagged the identical fact pattern as a live, unresolved document ambiguity (verifierb-01) and had to choose a reading rather than cite a settled resolution. An implementer built from B alone has no textual anchor forcing the experimental-range reading without independently deriving it from F35/F36 plus the established-violation-priority rule — and B's own in-house walk, performing that derivation, still declined to treat the case as settled.
findings.quotation_a: "...carrying no top-level record of a type it does not implement with MUST_UNDERSTAND = 1 — in a conforming file such a type is necessarily from the experimental range, since a reserved-range type carrying MU = 1 is itself a violation — and none of whose values exceeds the minimum guarantees of §21's limits table..."
findings.quotation_b: "...carrying no top-level record of a type it does not implement with MUST_UNDERSTAND = 1 and none of whose values exceeds the minimum guarantees of §21's limits table (§21.9), and MUST handle every codec and filter that §17 designates as core..."
findings.byte_level_rationale: Built from A alone, an implementer is told directly that an unimplemented-type/MU=1 record in an otherwise-violation-free file is necessarily experimental-range, so the two-branch report (experimental -> cannot establish; reserved -> nonconforming) follows without hedging. Built from B alone, nothing states this; a careful implementer who does not independently chain F35/F36 with R-CNF-11's priority rule has no textual anchor for the experimental-range reading, and as verifier-B's own transcript demonstrates on this exact scenario, can and does conclude the document leaves the case undetermined — producing a report that flags indeterminacy rather than one that states a settled two-branch answer. That is a difference in what the verifier's output says, not merely in its internal reasoning.

findings.title: The five cannot-establish grounds are stated once in each edition, but at different locations
findings.detail: A's §2.3 R-CNF-11 bullet enumerates the five cannot-establish grounds inline ('...as when the file names a format major version it does not implement, when a record carries MUST_UNDERSTAND = 1...'). B's §2.3 bullet instead says '(§21.6 names the grounds)', and the same five grounds, in matching wording, appear in B's own §21.6 — a paragraph edition A does not have at that location at all (grep -n "unable to check a requirement on a capability" hits only in spec/tarn.md, line 3934). Each edition states the five grounds exactly once; only the location moved. This is why verifiera-01's and verifierb-01's own citations of 'the five grounds' land in different sections of their respective editions.
findings.quotation_a: "...the last where some requirement is one it is unable to check on a capability or resource ground, as when the file names a format major version it does not implement, when a record carries MUST_UNDERSTAND = 1 with a type it does not implement (§21.6), when it cannot execute a codec or filter ([R-COD-11]), when it declines a layer's or a tile's decode on resource grounds and so cannot check §14's decoded-content obligations ([R-ERR-04], [R-SER-05], [R-SER-08]), or when it declines to decode a user-metadata document ([R-MTA-09])."
findings.quotation_b: (§2.3) "...the last where some requirement is one it is unable to check on a capability or resource ground (§21.6 names the grounds)." (§21.6) "A verifier is unable to check a requirement on a capability or resource ground, and so reports *cannot establish* ([R-CNF-11]), as when the file names a format major version it does not implement, a record carries MUST_UNDERSTAND = 1 with a type it does not implement, it cannot execute a codec or filter ([R-COD-11], §17.4), it declines a layer's or a tile's decode on resource grounds and so cannot check §14's decoded-content obligations ([R-ERR-04], [R-SER-05], [R-SER-08]), or it declines to decode a user-metadata document ([R-MTA-09])."
findings.byte_level_rationale: Net content is unchanged between editions; both state the identical five grounds exactly once. No implementation built from either edition alone would differ in behavior from this relocation alone — it affects only where a reader of the full document finds the list, not what the list says.

findings.title: verifiera-01's ambiguity (no sixth cannot-establish ground for a file-scope resource decline) is present unchanged in edition B
findings.detail: verifiera-01 (edition A's own walk) flags that §21.9/R-ERR-04 licenses a reader to decline on resource grounds 'at the whole file... before the directory can even be parsed', yet this specific case is never named as an explicit sixth ground alongside the illustrative five. §21.9's first ~120 lines diff byte-for-byte identical between editions, and per cmp-verifier-02 the five-grounds list's content is identical (only its location differs). The gap verifier-A surfaced therefore exists, unchanged, in edition B as well — it is a property of the shared specification text, not something either edition introduces or removes relative to the other.
findings.quotation_a: "...and MUST NOT certify a file it reports that way" / §21.9: "...at the whole file... as layers per file and dir_length are" (R-ERR-04's licence, confirmed identical to B by direct diff of §21.9's first ~120 lines)
findings.quotation_b: §21.9's corresponding passage, confirmed identical to A by direct diff (same R-ERR-04 licence text, same absence of a named sixth cannot-establish ground)
findings.byte_level_rationale: Since the governing passages diff identical between editions, no implementation built from A alone would differ from one built from B alone on this point — both face the identical unstated case.

findings.title: verifierb-02's observation (an undetectable fixed-declaration change) is a shared design property, not B-specific
findings.detail: verifierb-02 (edition B's own walk) observes that a commit silently changing a stored layer's fixed declaration is, by design, often undetectable by any verifier, because the bar binds the commit as an actor (no register row) and the verifier only ever walks the live state in one pass. Both governing passages — the full §20.3 step 4 bar paragraph and §9.7's closing Note ('Nothing here enumerates prior commits...') — diff byte-for-byte identical between editions. verifier-A's own V5 answer, reasoning independently from edition A alone, reaches the identical conclusion without citing this as a separate finding. This is a shared design property reachable from either edition, not a B-only discovery.
findings.quotation_a: "This bar binds the commit as an actor: no file is nonconforming by virtue of its violation, and no register row records the violation itself..." / "Nothing here enumerates prior commits. A verifier certifies what a reader can reach and counts what it cannot, which is decidable from the live trailer in one pass and does not depend on reconstructing the file's history..."
findings.quotation_b: Identical text, confirmed by direct diff of both passages against edition A (no difference).
findings.byte_level_rationale: Both passages are verbatim-identical between editions, so an implementation built from either alone exhibits the identical undetectability property; nothing about this is edition-specific.

findings.title: A states a closed list of three writer-conduct-only carve-outs with a completeness claim; B keeps only the abstract category
findings.detail: A's first §2.3 bullet names three specific instances of writer-conduct-only obligations that never make a file nonconforming (a set ignore-lane flag bit, a pre-trailer gap longer than the minimum pad, and the §20.3 step 4 fixed-declaration bar), introduced as 'are the cases this text states' — a completeness claim that these are the only such instances in the document. B's corresponding sentence drops both the enumeration and the completeness claim, stating only the bare disjunctive category. I checked each of the three instances at its own local section in both editions: the ignore-lane statement ('not a file-conformance violation'), the pre-trailer-pad statement ('a longer gap is conforming'), and the §20.3 step 4 bar (confirmed identical under cmp-verifier-04/V5) are all independently and identically recoverable in B. What is lost is the single place asserting completeness over the whole document, not the individual facts.
findings.quotation_a: "...§6.3's flags rules against a set ignore-lane bit (a creator's flags = 0, and an updater's copy-forward and set-no-other, §20.3 step 6 and §20.5), §6.2's pre-trailer gap longer than [R-LIF-02] step 5's pad, and §20.3 step 4's bar on the fixed declarations of a layer that stores a tile are the cases this text states, and each is declared where it arises rather than enumerated here."
findings.quotation_b: "A writer obligation that governs conduct rather than output, or whose violation this specification expressly declares not to be a file-conformance violation, binds the writer and never makes a file nonconforming."
findings.byte_level_rationale: Each of the three named instances survives, in substance, at its own local section in both editions (confirmed by direct comparison), so no byte-level divergence in verifier output is demonstrated on the facts given; the loss is the explicit closed-list/completeness assertion itself, which an implementer who reads only §2.3 (rather than the whole document) would miss in B but not in A.

findings.title: A's note that §20.4 preservation duties cover every record type is redundant with §20.4's own opening, identical in both editions
findings.detail: A's 'conforming updater' bullet adds '— which govern every record type, not only those it does not understand' after citing §20.4's preservation obligations; B drops the clause. §20.4's own opening sentence ('Persistence governs every record type; only the authoritative source of the flags differs') diffs identical between editions, so the scope claim A's §2.3 bullet previews is fully and identically restated at its point of full definition in both editions. A's §2.3 clause was a redundant forward-pointer, not unique content.
findings.quotation_a: "...as a rewriter writes a new one from it (§20.1), without necessarily understanding all of its content. An updater MUST satisfy every writer requirement for the bytes it produces, and additionally MUST honor the preservation obligations of §20.4 — which govern every record type, not only those it does not understand."
findings.quotation_b: "...as a rewriter writes a new one from it, without necessarily understanding all of its content; its tiers, the appender and the rewriter, are §20.1's. An updater MUST satisfy every writer requirement for the bytes it produces, and additionally MUST honor the preservation obligations of §20.4."
findings.byte_level_rationale: §20.4's opening, identical in both editions, restates the dropped scope claim in full, so no implementation built from B alone would differ from one built from A alone on this point.

findings.title: Minor local prose consolidations (ignore-lane statement, pre-trailer-pad statement, unexamined/per-requirement wording) change nothing decided
findings.detail: Beyond the §2.3 differences above, three smaller rewordings were checked and found to change no rule: (1) the ignore-lane-bit 'not a file-conformance violation' statement is reworded between editions but states the identical rule; (2) the pre-trailer-pad 'a longer gap is conforming' statement is likewise reworded without changing the rule; (3) V1's per-requirement-report/unexamined clause is stated as two sentences in A and consolidated into one in B, covering the identical two obligations (the per-requirement report and *unexamined* both 'constrain the report, not the verdict'). All three were confirmed by direct line-range comparison, not inferred from the probes' matching answers alone.
findings.quotation_a: "...a writer creating a file under this text MUST write flags = 0, but a set ignore-lane bit is not a file-conformance violation..." / "...bounds their number only through step 5 of the commit protocol, which pads to the next 64-byte boundary ([R-LIF-02]) — a longer gap is conforming, and no conforming commit produces one." / "...that per-requirement report constrains the report and not the verdict, as *unexamined* does below. ... *Unexamined* is neither a verdict nor *cannot establish* — it constrains the report, not the verdict."
findings.quotation_b: "...so a writer creating a file under this text MUST write flags = 0. A set ignore-lane bit is nevertheless not a file-conformance violation..." / "...and bounds its length only through step 5 of the commit protocol, which pads to the next 64-byte boundary ([R-LIF-02]); a longer gap is conforming, though no conforming commit produces one." / "...A verifier MAY stop at the first violation it finds; one that does MUST report each scope it did not examine as *unexamined*... *Unexamined* is neither a verdict nor *cannot establish*; it and the per-requirement report constrain the report, not the verdict."
findings.byte_level_rationale: Each pair states the identical rule under different sentence boundaries; no implementation built from either edition alone would diverge in behavior or in report content from these rewordings.

findings.location_a: §3.3 'Container and array model' (A lines 435-442, the whole subsection) and §1 Introduction, final paragraph (A lines 90-94, 'Reading this document')
findings.title: Part I/Part II architectural-independence claim dropped entirely, stated twice in A, nowhere in B
findings.detail: A makes, twice, the claim that Part I (the container) is independent of Part II (the array model) by construction: §3.3's Note says 'no Part I structure requires decoding sample payloads, so appenders, and rewriters that carry a layer forward, operate on files whose layers they cannot decode,' calling this 'load-bearing for the updater rules of §7 and §20.' The Introduction separately says 'Part I alone yields a container reader — one that opens files, walks the directory, and lists layers without decoding a sample; returning sample values needs Part II as well.' B has neither: §3.3 has no heading or body in B at all, and B's rewritten Introduction closing paragraph talks instead about the document's own writing rubric (purpose/layout-table/writer-rules/... ). An implementer of a partial, container-only tool (e.g. a directory lister, or an updater that relocates layers it cannot decode) reading B alone has no textual basis for the claim that this is architecturally sound rather than a lucky accident of the format; A states it as a design invariant twice.
findings.quotation_a: Note. Part I (container) is independent of Part II (array model) by construction: no Part I structure requires decoding sample payloads, so appenders, and rewriters that carry a layer forward, operate on files whose layers they cannot decode — that independence is load-bearing for the updater rules of §7 and §20. [§3.3] / Part I alone yields a container reader — one that opens files, walks the directory, and lists layers without decoding a sample; returning sample values needs Part II as well, since §19.3's layer validation resolves into Part II's value sets and geometry rules at every step. [§1]
findings.quotation_b: absent
findings.byte_level_rationale: Both statements are explicitly non-normative (the §3.3 one is inside a Note, the Introduction is excluded from normative text by §2.1/R-CNF-01 in both editions). No conformance class, requirement ID, or register row in either edition depends on this claim; a reader or updater built from B alone would still correctly implement every Part I/Part II rule, since those are stated independently and identically in both editions' §5-§10 and §11-§18. This is a loss of architectural guidance/rationale useful to an implementer deciding what to build, not of a rule that changes bytes emitted or accept/reject verdicts.

findings.location_a: §2.4 Outcome classes and owning scope, A lines 300-304
findings.title: Dropped clarification that preserve-verbatim is orthogonal to reader-side 'ignore', with no restatement
findings.detail: A states, in ordinary normative prose (not inside a Note): 'The same vocabulary is used for defined conditions that are not violations (an unknown ancillary record is ignored, not rejected). preserve-verbatim names an updater obligation, orthogonal to reader outcomes: a record a reader ignores can still be one an updater preserves.' This sentence bridges two rules that otherwise live in different sections — §21.5's reader-side ignore-record outcome and §20.4's updater-side preserve-verbatim obligation — and heads off the natural misreading that a reader-ignored record is one any tool, updater included, may silently drop. B's §2.4 omits this passage entirely; I found no restatement of the orthogonality claim anywhere else in B (both §20.4 and §21.5 remain byte-identical to A, but neither of them, alone, states that the two concepts are independent axes).
findings.quotation_a: The same vocabulary is used for defined conditions that are not violations (an unknown ancillary record is *ignored*, not rejected). **preserve-verbatim** names an updater obligation, orthogonal to reader outcomes: a record a reader ignores can still be one an updater preserves.
findings.quotation_b: absent
findings.byte_level_rationale: The two rules this sentence connects (ignore-record's definition and preserve-verbatim's updater obligation) are each fully and identically stated elsewhere in both editions (§21.5, §20.4), so an implementation built correctly from either edition's full text would still implement both correctly. What's missing is the explicit bridge preventing a careless cross-reading; it does not itself add or remove a requirement on bytes.

findings.location_a: §2.4 Outcome classes and owning scope, trailing Note, A lines 339-340
findings.title: Note clarifying 'reject' means scope of unusability, not UI, dropped with no restatement
findings.detail: A's §2.4 ends with 'Note. "Reject" prescribes the scope of unusability, not user interface: how failure is reported is implementation technique.' This disambiguates the outcome-class vocabulary (reject-file/-layer/-tile) against a plausible misreading that 'reject' mandates some error-reporting mechanism. B drops this Note; I confirmed by grep that the phrase 'implementation technique' appears in B only at the unrelated, already-present §2.1 Note about requirement phrasing discipline (present identically in both editions), not in connection with 'reject' specifically.
findings.quotation_a: **Note.** "Reject" prescribes the scope of unusability, not user interface: how failure is reported is implementation technique.
findings.quotation_b: absent
findings.byte_level_rationale: The note is explicitly about implementation technique (how failure is reported), which by the spec's own framework never affects bytes emitted or accept/reject verdicts. Its removal changes no requirement; it is purely interpretive guidance for the term 'reject' that is now undocumented in B.

findings.location_a: §2.3 Conformance classes, A lines 183-184 (inside the R-CNF-03 paragraph)
findings.title: Derived consequence about unimplemented-type MU=1 records being necessarily experimental-range is dropped, unrestated
findings.detail: A's R-CNF-03 paragraph includes the aside 'in a conforming file such a type is necessarily from the experimental range, since a reserved-range type carrying MU = 1 is itself a violation.' This is a valid derived consequence of R-CNT-15/R-CNT-18 (reserved-range type + MU=1 is itself a violation), which remain stated identically in both editions' register rows (F35, L24). B's R-CNF-03 paragraph omits this derived clause; I found no restatement elsewhere.
findings.quotation_a: carrying no top-level record of a type it does not implement with MUST_UNDERSTAND = 1 — in a conforming file such a type is necessarily from the experimental range, since a reserved-range type carrying MU = 1 is itself a violation — and none of whose values exceeds the minimum guarantees of §21's limits table
findings.quotation_b: carrying no top-level record of a type it does not implement with MUST_UNDERSTAND = 1 and none of whose values exceeds the minimum guarantees of §21's limits table (§21.9)
findings.byte_level_rationale: This is an explanatory consequence drawn from two other requirements (R-CNT-15, R-CNT-18) that are unchanged and identical in both editions' register tables; an implementer who applies those two rules correctly reaches the same conclusion with or without this aside stating it explicitly. Low materiality; flagged for completeness per the charter's instruction to track every item A decides, even derived ones, but this does not change any byte or verdict.

findings.location_a: §2.3 Conformance classes, trailing Note, A lines 283-290
findings.title: Three-row worked illustration of the format-major 'reach' test (F14/F5/F15) dropped with no restatement
findings.detail: A closes §2.3 with a Note walking through three concrete register rows to illustrate why the 'reach' test (whether a condition applies to a file declaring a non-1 format major) turns on the invariant a check asserts rather than the bytes it reads: F14 reaches despite reading redefinable bytes (because it only asserts the fixed CRC-32C invariant), F5 does not reach despite checking the physical file size (because its 128-byte-floor derivation is major-1-specific), and F15 does not reach despite citing R-CNT-24 (because the specific zero bytes it checks are inside the 48 a future major may redefine). B's rewritten §2.3 states the general rule but drops this worked illustration entirely; I found no restatement of this three-row walkthrough elsewhere, though the underlying per-row 'reach' determinations are presumably still recorded in the §21.2 register table itself (a table, outside my remit to re-verify).
findings.quotation_a: **Note.** The test is the invariant a condition violates, not the fields it reads, and three rows show why the distinction carries the weight. §21.2's F14 reaches although the bytes it checksums include fields a future major may redefine: it consumes them as CRC input and asserts only `[R-CNT-24]`'s CRC-32C at F − 4 over [F − 64, F − 4). F5 does not reach although its subject is the physical file size, which no major can redefine: the 128-byte floor it asserts is derived from a directory of at least 4 bytes at an offset of at least 16 and a 64-aligned F (`[R-CNT-27]`), and those are format major 1's. F15 does not reach although its Governing rule cell cites `[R-CNT-24]`: the trailer bytes it requires be zero are inside the 48 that rule lets a future major redefine.
findings.quotation_b: absent
findings.byte_level_rationale: This is explicitly a Note (non-normative in both editions under R-CNF-01) that illustrates, rather than states, the reach rule; the rule itself (R-CNF-13) and the per-row determinations it illustrates are unaffected and, so far as the register table (outside this sweep's remit) records them, presumably unchanged. Flagged because it is a worked figure A provides and B drops entirely, per the charter's instruction to track worked figures, but it does not change any byte emitted or verdict reached.

findings.location_b: absent (no section 3.3 heading or content anywhere in B)
findings.title: B drops A's entire section 3.3 Note on Part I/Part II independence, unrestated anywhere
findings.detail: A's section 3.3 consists of a single Note: Part I (container) is independent of Part II (array model) 'by construction: no Part I structure requires decoding sample payloads, so appenders, and rewriters that carry a layer forward, operate on files whose layers they cannot decode', and calls that independence 'load-bearing for the updater rules of section 7 and section 20'. B has no section 3.3 heading at all - section 3.1 and 3.2 are immediately followed by section 2 Conformance. A full-file grep in B for the distinguishing phrases 'independent of Part', 'load-bearing' (beyond one unrelated hit), and 'cannot decode' returns zero matches tied to this content. The underlying permission (an updater need not decode a layer's payload to carry it forward) is nonetheless fully and identically established elsewhere by section 20's writer-tier and re-emission rules, which are byte-identical between editions, so this is reported as a content omission rather than a byte-level loss: A itself marks this block as a Note, i.e. already non-normative, and no [R-xxx] identifier or register row depends on it.
findings.quotation_a: > **Note.** Part I (container) is independent of Part II (array model) by construction: no Part I structure requires decoding sample payloads, so appenders, and rewriters that carry a layer forward, operate on files whose layers they cannot decode — that independence is load-bearing for the updater rules of §7 and §20.
findings.quotation_b: absent
findings.byte_level_rationale: The claim is rationale for a permission that section 20's writer-tier and re-emission rules (section 20.1, section 20.4) state directly and operatively, and those sections are byte-identical between A and B. An implementation built from B alone reaches the identical conclusion about what an appender or rewriter may do with an undecodable layer; no requirement ID or register row cites section 3.3, so its removal changes no conformance test outcome.

findings.title: B's Introduction drops A's Part I/II/III roadmap paragraph, restating the same independence theme a second time with no B counterpart
findings.detail: A's Introduction has a paragraph beginning 'Reading this document. section 2 fixes the conformance vocabulary...' that walks through Part I/II/III and states 'Part I alone yields a container reader — one that opens files, walks the directory, and lists layers without decoding a sample; returning sample values needs Part II as well, since section 19.3's layer validation resolves into Part II's value sets and geometry rules at every step.' B's Introduction has a differently-scoped 'How to read this document' paragraph (about rubric and layout-table columns, matching content moved from A's top-of-document Note) but contains no counterpart to the Part I/II/III roadmap sentence. A full-file grep in B for 'without decoding', 'Part I (§5', 'yields a container reader', and 'fixes the conformance vocabulary' returns zero hits. This is the same substantive idea as adv-01 (Part I needs no decoding to function), asserted a second time in A and dropped a second time in B with no restatement.
findings.quotation_a: Part I alone yields a container reader — one that opens files, walks the directory, and lists layers without decoding a sample; returning sample values needs Part II as well, since §19.3's layer validation resolves into Part II's value sets and geometry rules at every step.
findings.quotation_b: absent
findings.byte_level_rationale: Purely descriptive roadmap prose with no requirement ID attached in either edition; the only testable fact it implies (a container-only reader can list layers without decoding samples) is independently guaranteed by section 19.1's open algorithm and section 19.3's layer access rules, both byte-identical between editions.

findings.location_a: section 3.1 Terms, 'addressed tile / stored tile' bullet
findings.location_b: section 3.1 Terms, 'addressed tile / stored tile' bullet
findings.title: B's glossary makes 'addressed tile' explicitly generation-relative; A states it as an unconditional property of the layer
findings.detail: A defines the term as 'every tile of a layer is *addressed*' with no generation qualifier, then separately qualifies 'stored' as generation-relative. B instead defines 'addressed' itself as generation-relative: 'a tile is *addressed* in a generation if that generation's tile index has an entry for it: the tiles of the layer's grid under the geometry that generation declares'. This matters because dimension extents can grow across generations (confirmed elsewhere in both editions, e.g. the append procedure's growth rules), so the set of tiles that exist in a layer's grid is not fixed for all generations of a layer - A's literal wording ('every tile of a layer is addressed', unqualified) is imprecise about which generation's grid is meant, while B's wording resolves that ambiguity explicitly. Neither edition attaches a requirement ID to this glossary bullet, and the operative rules that actually determine which tiles exist for a given generation (section 11.2 Grid arithmetic, section 15 Tile Index, and the growth clause of section 20.3's append procedure) are byte-identical between editions, so no concrete file's conformance verdict changes.
findings.quotation_a: **addressed tile / stored tile** — every tile of a layer is *addressed*. A tile is *stored in a generation* if and only if that generation's tile-index entry for it is not the sentinel (§15); unqualified *stored* means stored in the live generation.
findings.quotation_b: **addressed tile / stored tile** — a tile is *addressed* in a generation if that generation's tile index has an entry for it: the tiles of the layer's grid under the geometry that generation declares (§11.2, §15). It is *stored in a generation* if and only if that entry is not the sentinel (§15); unqualified *stored* means stored in the live generation.
findings.byte_level_rationale: This is glossary prose, not a cited requirement; the byte-level determination of which tiles are addressed for any given generation is made entirely by section 11.2, section 15 and section 20.3's growth clause, all three confirmed byte-identical between A and B, so a reader or verifier built from either edition's operative rules alone computes the identical addressed-tile set for any concrete file and generation.

findings.title: No outcome class or operational guidance when a reader lacks an assigned, core codec/filter it is obliged to implement
findings.quotation_a: "software that declines to support a core codec, a core filter, either channel layout, a core sample type, an assigned user-metadata encoding, or a registered record type is not a conforming reader, even if it reads all other conforming files correctly"
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.detail: For a layer whose codec (or filter, channel layout, sample type, metadata encoding, or registered record type) is an assigned/core value a reader cannot execute, the document assigns no outcome class and states no operational constraint on that software's behavior, unlike the explicit reject-layer outcome (L43) it gives for a reserved/experimental codec value or the cannot-establish outcome (R-COD-11) it gives a verifier. Two implementations both encounter a conforming file whose single layer declares codec 3 (zstd), and neither implements zstd. One refuses the whole file; the other serves every other layer and even returns this layer's declared geometry/channel list while reporting the tile reads as failed. Both are equally 'not a conforming reader' under R-CNF-03, and the document gives no basis to prefer one behavior over the other, because it deliberately stops regulating behavior once the premise (a conforming reader) is false, rather than through any gap in what it says about conforming readers.
findings.byte_level_rationale: Resolving this either way changes nothing about what bytes a conforming implementation may emit or must accept/reject, since by definition every conforming reader already implements all four core codecs (R-CNF-03) and this scenario never arises for one; the question only affects how one characterizes the unconstrained behavior of software the specification has already excluded from its reader obligations, which is a documentation/implementer-guidance observation rather than a determinable byte-level divergence.

findings.title: No outcome class exists for a reader that cannot execute an assigned core codec/filter
findings.detail: R-CNF-03 requires every conforming reader to implement all four codecs and both filters ('no subset profiles... even if it reads all other conforming files correctly'). R-COD-11/§17.4 then state that the reject-layer outcome for an unexecutable codec/filter 'arises only at a reserved or experimental value' for a conforming reader -- i.e. the document treats 'conforming reader lacking a core codec' as a contradiction in terms, never a case needing a defined outcome. An implementer building a reader that supports most of the format but, say, not zstd yet, gets no guidance: no register row, no §21.6 non-violation entry, nothing says whether it may reject just that layer, must refuse the whole file, or is simply undefined software. Byte-level test: does resolving this change what bytes a conforming implementation may emit or must accept/reject? No -- by the document's own terms no conforming implementation is ever in this state, so no conforming implementation's required behavior is left undetermined; what is left undetermined is the behavior of software the document declines to call a reader at all.
findings.quotation_a: For a conforming reader that position arises only at a reserved or experimental value, every assigned codec and filter being core: it rejects the layer (R-COD-03, R-COD-09); software unable to execute an assigned codec or filter is not a conforming reader (R-CNF-03).
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: No conforming implementation is ever in the described state (lacking a core codec while being conforming), by the document's own closed-core design (§1, R-CNF-03), so resolving this gap would not change any byte a conforming reader must accept, reject, or emit -- it would only supply guidance for software the document already excludes from its conformance classes.

findings.location_a: S20.3 step 4 (fixed-declaration bar for a layer that stored a tile) and R-CNF-02's conduct-rule framing
findings.title: A disallowed fill-only commit's file-conformance consequence is conditional on padding, not automatic
findings.detail: S20.3 step 4 forbids an appender from changing only a layer's fill value once the layer has stored a tile, listing "a fill change" explicitly among excluded operations, and frames the bar as binding "the commit as an actor" rather than the file (on the R-CNF-02 conduct-rule model: "no file is nonconforming by virtue of its violation"). It then adds that "a file such a commit leaves can be nonconforming on its own terms" - without stating when. Tracing the only register row this could land on (T4, padding positions must encode the channel's recorded fill, S14.5/R-SER-05), the resulting file is actually nonconforming only if the layer has at least one padding position (some dimension's extent not an exact multiple of its tile extent); a layer with no padding at all (extents exactly tiled) would have its already-stored bytes pass every other check unchanged, and the resulting file would remain fully conforming despite the writer having breached S20.3's conduct bar - an implementer reading the probe's framing ("is the file nonconforming?") as a yes/no would reasonably but wrongly answer unconditionally.
findings.quotation_a: "This bar binds the commit as an actor: no file is nonconforming by virtue of its violation, and no register row records the violation itself … a file such a commit leaves can be nonconforming on its own terms, as the paragraph below sets out."
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: It changes whether a verifier may certify the output file at all: with padding present, the stale fill bytes are a detectable T4 violation a verifier must act on (reject-layer); with no padding, the identical fill-only commit yields bytes that pass certification, so whether this condition is read as present or absent in a given file directly changes the accept/reject verdict a conforming verifier must render over the same class of writer misbehavior.

findings.location_a: S20.4, opening paragraphs of "Re-emission and preservation"
findings.title: A tool's self-classification as "implementing" a type, not that type's own MU bit, decides whether it may drop the type's records
findings.detail: The preservation table's MU=1 row ("Retain byte-identical … never silently deletable") is stated as reaching "only a type the updater does not implement," so for any type the updater implements - whether registered by this specification or implemented from an entirely external, third-party definition that itself fixes MU=1/PE=0 - "only the PE bit bites," meaning the record is treated under the MU=0/PE=0 row (may be dropped) regardless of what that external definition calls its own MU bit. The practical effect: the same bytes, the same record type, can be either "never drop" or "may drop, SHOULD report" purely according to whether the processing tool happens to implement the type - a classifier the tool applies to itself - rather than according to the type's own declared criticality. This is explicit in the text (not a contradiction), but it is the kind of load-bearing fork (which class a tool self-reports into) that is easy to misread as the type's own flags controlling the outcome directly.
findings.quotation_a: "For a type the updater implements that this specification does not register, the definition it implements the type from supplies the flags, and the stored bits never do … Its MU = 1 row reaches only a type the updater does not implement — an updater implements both registered types and understands an unregistered type it implements from its definition … so for an implemented type only the PE bit bites."
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: It directly decides whether a record's bytes survive a commit or rewrite: under the MU=1 reading an implementer might wrongly conclude the record must never be dropped (since the type's own definition calls it MU=1); under the document's actual rule, an updater that implements the type may drop an unmodified instance of it in any commit or rewrite, licensed exactly as an ordinary MU=0/PE=0 ancillary record - a difference of whether specific bytes appear in the output at all.

findings.location_a: §2.3 Conformance classes (Conforming updater bullet) vs. §2.3 (Conforming verifier bullet, 'Verifiers and updaters are readers...')
findings.title: Updater's content-understanding floor conflicts with 'inherits every reader obligation'
findings.detail: §2.3 defines a conforming updater as working 'without necessarily understanding all of its content,' which would seem to exempt it from R-CNF-03's no-subset-profiles requirement that a conforming reader implement all four codecs, both filters, both layouts and all thirteen sample types. But the same section's verifier bullet asserts 'Verifiers and updaters are readers of the files they process and inherit every reader obligation' -- and R-CNF-03's capability floor is textually a reader obligation. Appendix H's non-normative 'Conforming updater' checklist never lists full sample-type/codec coverage, which favors a narrow reading of 'obligation' (behavioral MUSTs only), but no normative sentence states that narrowing. An implementer building a rewriter for layers whose sample type it has not implemented (W8's exact premise) gets different answers depending on which reading controls: under the broad reading such a tool cannot be a conforming updater at all when it meets such a layer (it must refuse everything, full stop); under the narrow reading it may carry the layer forward unmodified subject only to checksum verification, as I answered in probe W8.
findings.quotation_a: "A tool that modifies an existing file, or as a rewriter writes a new one from it, without necessarily understanding all of its content... Verifiers and updaters are readers of the files they process and inherit every reader obligation."
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: The two readings produce different legal actions for the same input bytes and the same tool: under the broad reading, a rewriter lacking one core sample type must refuse to rewrite any file containing such a layer (emits nothing); under the narrow reading it may carry that layer's tiles forward verbatim after checksum verification (emits the same bytes, relocated). Which bytes a conforming implementation may legally produce for this input differs between the two readings.

findings.location_b: §20.4 (preservation table's governing-flags paragraph and its PE-bit-alone sentence)
findings.title: Literal MU=1/PE=0-as-PE=1 coercion vs. 'the definition supplies the flags, stored bits never do'
findings.detail: R-CNT-12 states, without qualification by record type or registration status, that 'a reader or updater encountering [MU=1 with PE=0] MUST treat the record as PE = 1 (never silently deletable).' §20.4 states that for a type an updater implements from an external, unregistered definition, that definition's flags govern and 'the stored bits never do,' and that for any implemented type 'only the PE bit bites' -- which, for W11's scenario (definition fixes MU=1/PE=0), licenses dropping the record under the PE=0 obligation rather than treating it as never-deletable. If a compliant writer of such a record stores the literal bit pattern MU=1/PE=0 on disk (the natural consequence of following the external definition at face value), the two rules prescribe opposite updater behavior for the same bytes: R-CNT-12 says treat as PE=1 (preserve forever); §20.4 says treat under PE=0 (droppable). The document never states which rule controls this overlap, nor what bit pattern a compliant writer of such a type should actually emit.
findings.quotation_a: "Writers MUST NOT emit the combination MU = 1 with PE = 0; a reader or updater encountering it MUST treat the record as PE = 1 (never silently deletable)."
findings.quotation_b: "For a type the updater implements that this specification does not register, the definition it implements the type from supplies the flags, and the stored bits never do... so for an implemented type only the PE bit bites."
findings.byte_level_rationale: The resolution directly decides whether an updater may legally drop such a record in a commit: under R-CNT-12's literal reading it may never drop it; under §20.4's reading it may drop it in any commit it is otherwise free to make. These are different sets of legally emittable output bytes for the same input.

findings.title: W8's 'unimplemented sample type' premise strains against the core-type conformance floor
findings.detail: §12.1 states 'This specification defines exactly thirteen sample types, all core: a conforming reader MUST decode every one of them, and none is skippable,' and L34 makes any other channel-type value itself a layer-scope violation. A scenario positing a rewriter that 'cannot decode' a layer's sample type is therefore only coherent for a tool operating under the narrower 'conforming updater' floor (which does not require full reader-capability coverage per §2.3's own wording) rather than as a 'conforming reader' in the §2.3/R-CNF-03 sense -- a distinction the document draws but does not explicitly reconcile with the adjacent 'inherits every reader obligation' sentence (see writerb-01). This is not itself a defect, but it means any answer to W8 is implicitly resting on resolving writerb-01's ambiguity in the narrow direction.
findings.quotation_a: "This specification defines exactly thirteen sample types, all core: a conforming reader MUST decode every one of them, and none is skippable."
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: Whether such a tool can exist as a conforming updater at all changes what it may legally do with the input bytes (refuse everything vs. carry the layer forward), making this directly relevant to, rather than separate from, the byte-level stakes already described under writerb-01.

findings.title: A commit's forbidden fill-value change is explicitly unwitnessed -- no register row, no detectable byte trace
findings.detail: The document is unusually forthright about this: the bar on changing a stored layer's fill (among other fixed declarations) via commit is stated to be a pure writer-conduct rule, carrying 'no register row,' and the very next paragraph explains that essentially none of the checksums in §8 can see it -- only a short, explicitly named list of structurally-constrained content (padding positions, pad bits, boolean bytes, and codec-framing checks under a changed codec/filter) has a register row at all, and a plain fill-value change is not on that list. Under §21.7's own stated test for detectability, this makes a fill-only change in violation of §20.3 step 4 an unwitnessed condition: a verifier built strictly from §21's register cannot distinguish a file that underwent this forbidden change from one that reached the same bytes by a legitimate rewrite. This is internally consistent (not a contradiction) but is a sharp, easily-missed consequence worth surfacing for anyone implementing a verifier under the assumption that §21's register is exhaustive over 'what writers must not do.'
findings.quotation_a: "This bar binds the commit as an actor: no file is nonconforming by virtue of its violation, and no register row records the violation itself... with every checksum in §8 certifying the result and, but for [a short named list]... no check any actor owes able to see it."
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: This does not change what bytes an implementation must accept or reject -- it is a correct and already-explicit statement that no such byte-level check exists for this condition, which is exactly the document's own §21.7 test working as designed, not an unresolved question about bytes.

findings.title: No cannot-establish ground is explicitly named for a file-scope resource decline
findings.detail: [R-CNF-11] states the general rule for cannot-establish ('some requirement is one it is unable to check on a capability or resource ground') and then an illustrative, 'as when' list of five grounds: unimplemented format major, unimplemented MU=1 type, unexecutable codec/filter, resource-declined layer/tile decode, declined user-metadata document. Separately, §21.9/[R-ERR-04] licenses a reader (hence a verifier) to decline on resource grounds 'at the whole file ... as layers per file and dir_length are' -- i.e. before the directory can even be parsed, with no layer or tile yet in view. The document never says, for that specific file-scope case, whether the resulting report is cannot-establish (reached only via the general rule, not any of the five named grounds) or falls outside the three-verdict vocabulary entirely. An implementer following only the five named grounds could build a verifier that has no defined report shape for an oversized directory/layer-count file it never got into; one reading the general rule literally would report cannot-establish, naming [R-ERR-04] and the exceeded quantity.
findings.quotation_a: "the last where some requirement is one it is unable to check on a capability or resource ground, as when the file names a format major version it does not implement, when a record carries MUST_UNDERSTAND = 1 with a type it does not implement (§21.6), when it cannot execute a codec or filter ([R-COD-11]), when it declines a layer's or a tile's decode on resource grounds ... ([R-ERR-04] ...), or when it declines to decode a user-metadata document ([R-MTA-09])" ... "a reader MAY decline it: at the whole file, or at the narrowest scope ... be that a layer, a tile, the record carrying a user-metadata document ... or the file itself where the quantity is the file's, as layers per file and dir_length are"
findings.quotation_b: n/a
findings.byte_level_rationale: It decides whether a conforming verifier's output for a file exceeding a file-scope guarantee (dir_length or layer count) must use the word 'cannot establish' plus name [R-ERR-04] and the exceeded quantity per [R-CNF-11]'s reporting duty, or may instead emit a differently-shaped refusal outside the three-verdict vocabulary -- a real difference in what text/fields a conforming verifier implementation must emit for the same bytes.

findings.title: Probe scenario (unimplemented top-level type, MU=1) is bimodal: verdict depends on reserved- vs experimental-range, unstated by the probe
findings.location_b: section 7.2 [R-CNT-15]; section 21.6 closing paragraphs (experimental-range MU=1 exception); register rows F35/F36 (section 21.2)
findings.quotation_a: n/a
findings.quotation_b: A record at file scope whose type the reader does not implement is governed by its stored MU bit: MU = 1 is reject-file ... A type from the reserved range is a value this specification has not assigned. Emitting one is a violation ... / [21.6] An experimental-range top-level record type carrying MU = 1 ... [R-CNT-15] obliges the reader to reject, and [R-CNF-02] makes the file conforming all the same.
findings.detail: Given a bare description of "a top-level record of an unimplemented type with MU=1," the document itself routes the same fact pattern to two different verdicts depending on a detail the probe omits: whether the type value lies in the reserved range (0x0003-0x7FFF) or the experimental range (>=0x8000). An implementer who reads the scenario as reserved-range builds logic that reports nonconforming (F35 at open plus F36's independent violation for emitting the value at all); one who reads it as experimental-range builds logic that reports cannot-establish (no violation exists under [R-CNF-02]/section 21.6; the reader simply cannot proceed past the reject-file capability refusal). Both implementations are faithful to this document, yet they diverge on the verdict for byte patterns that fit the probe's English equally well, because the probe's own wording does not pin down the type's range.
findings.byte_level_rationale: Given identical bytes matching only "top-level record of an unimplemented type with MU=1," two conforming implementations built from this text alone diverge on the reported verdict (nonconforming vs cannot-establish) purely depending on which numeric range they assume the type occupies - a fact the probe's wording does not supply, though the document itself resolves the question once the range is known.

findings.title: A commit that silently changes a stored layer's fixed declaration is, by the document's own design, often undetectable by any verifier
findings.location_b: section 20.3 step 4 (fixed-declaration bar and its enumerated detectable/undetectable fallout list); section 9.7 closing Note; section 21.7
findings.quotation_a: n/a
findings.quotation_b: This bar binds the commit as an actor: no file is nonconforming by virtue of its violation, and no register row records the violation itself ... but for a stored tile's decoded size, a padding position or pad bit, or a boolean byte the register witnesses (T3, T14, T21, T22, T4, T5, T2) ... no check any actor owes able to see it.
findings.detail: An implementer who builds a verifier strictly from the register (sections 21.2-21.5) alone, without reading section 20.3's writer-conduct prose closely, might assume that changing a stored layer's fixed declaration (e.g. its fill value, or re-typing a channel to another type of the same element size) always leaves a detectable trace, since the register is billed as complete over detectable violations. The document explicitly carves out the opposite for exactly this family of changes: provided the change preserves decoded size and codec/filter framing, it is unwitnessed by construction, and the verifier - which only ever walks the live state in one pass and never compares generations - reports the file conforming even though the writer violated a conduct rule.
findings.byte_level_rationale: For a fixed-declaration change that preserves decoded size and codec/filter framing (e.g. a same-size re-type, a fill-value change), a conforming implementation emits/accepts the identical bytes whether or not the underlying writer-conduct rule was honored - the document itself names this as one of its exactly-enumerated undetectable-by-construction cases, which is a notable property worth surfacing even though the document determines (rather than fails to determine) the outcome.

groups.title: Forbidden fill/fixed-declaration change via commit: conduct-only bar, witnessed by T4 exactly when the layer has padding — one reporter misreads this as unconditionally unwitnessed

groups.location_b: B §20.3 step 4 (same passage, byte-identical); §21.7; T4 row (tarn.md:3814); §9.7 closing Note
groups.byte_level_rationale: Verified T4's row text is byte-identical in both editions: 'A padding position does not encode, for each channel it carries, that channel's recorded fill value.' A fill-only commit leaves old padding bytes stale; if the layer has >=1 padding position, those stale bytes now mismatch the newly-declared fill, which is exactly T4's condition — so the change IS witnessed whenever padding exists, and unwitnessed only when it does not (writera-01's correct conditional). writerb-04 reads the identical T-number list and the identical step-4 paragraph but asserts, unconditionally, that a fill change 'is in fact unwitnessed' and 'not in that named list' — misreading the very row that names it. A verifier following writerb-04's unconditional reading would skip T4 on a fill-only change and might certify as conforming a file a correct verifier would reject-layer for a stale padding byte, so this is a real, demonstrable difference in accept/reject verdict depending on which reading of the (edition-identical) text an implementer follows — hence byte-level, though the divergence is between two READINGS of identical text, not between editions.
groups.recommended_action: No change to either edition's text (both state the padding-conditional rule correctly and identically via T4 and the step-4 paragraph). Correct writerb-04's/verifierb-02's downstream report to state the conditional explicitly, matching writera-01's framing, rather than claiming unconditional unwitnessedness.
